name: Bronzers (caramel)

card.summary: Caramel bronzers are wash-off or gradual products that tint skin a warm tan shade to give an instantly sun-kissed look without UV exposure.
card.aka: face and body bronzer; DHA bronzer
card.note: Colour additive DHA is approved by FDA for external use only, not on lips, eyes or by inhalation.

quick.overview:
Bronzers are temporary skin colourants in powder, lotion, spray or mousse form that add a tan tone. Wikipedia notes that caramel is among common bronzer ingredients, and many products pair them with DHA self-tanners.

The appearance payoff is a warmer, more even skin tone that evens out pale or uneven skin and adds definition. Wash-off bronzers last until washing; DHA-based tans fade over a few days.
quick.how: Users apply them to face and body with a brush or hand, or spray. Wash-off bronzers suit one-day tans and can complement a DHA tan; uneven application can look orange or streaky.
quick.risks: Sunless tanning products do not provide UV protection. FDA advises against DHA near eyes, lips and mucous membranes, or inhaling it. Contact dermatitis from DHA and erythrulose is reported.

lead: Bronzers are temporary skin colourants sold as powders, sprays, mousses, gels, lotions and tinted moisturisers. They tint the surface of the skin much as makeup does and come off with soap and water; caramel, walnut-oil extract and jojoba extract are among the ingredients commonly used for the colour.[3][4] Some bronzers also contain dihydroxyacetone (DHA), the FDA-approved colour additive used in sunless tanners.[1]

People use bronzers to get a warm, golden-brown, sun-kissed look straight away, without UV exposure: a face-and-body tint for a single day or event, a deeper colour layered over a DHA self-tan, or a gradual tan built up by tinted lotions used daily.[4] The colour evens out pale or patchy skin and can add apparent definition to cheekbones, collarbones and muscle.

DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin to produce a brown tone that fades over roughly 3 to 10 days as that layer sheds.[3] A 2005 review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal describes DHA-based sprays, which are combined with bronzers and moisturisers, as a generally safe alternative for people who want a suntanned appearance.[2] Sunless tanners are regulated as cosmetics and cannot provide sun protection.[1]

chain: Skin takes on a warm tan tone
Even, sun-kissed appearance without UV exposure
angle.text: Bronzers colour the skin surface directly, so the effect is immediate for wash-off versions and develops over hours for DHA.

Cosmetic / colour additive (US); the term 'bronzer' is not legally defined[4]

paras: Wikipedia describes bronzers as a temporary form of sunless tanning. They come as powders, sprays, mousses, gels, lotions and moisturisers, and wash off with soap and water. The article notes that neither 'bronzer' nor 'sunless tanner' is a legally defined term in the United States.[4][3]

Three broad uses are described. Bronzers are often used for a one-day tan. They are applied on top of a DHA self-tanner to deepen the colour. And a newer category of moisturisers with a gradual tanning agent builds colour with repeated use, with a slight change visible after the first application.[4] Wash-off bronzers can rub onto clothing, though dark clothes hide it, and careless application can leave a splotchy or orange look.[4][3]
Common ingredients include caramel, walnut-oil extract and jojoba extract for colour, and many products also contain benzyl alcohol, tocopherol (vitamin E) and fragrance.[4]

Sunless tanners typically contain DHA at 3 to 5 percent. Wikipedia explains that DHA is not a dye, stain or paint: it reacts with amino acids in the stratum corneum, the dead outer layer of skin, and does not involve the skin's underlying melanin. The colour therefore fades as that layer exfoliates, over about 3 to 10 days.[3]

A 2018 review in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology describes DHA as a three-carbon sugar allowed by the FDA as a color additive in sunless tanning products and notes that bronzers, which are removed with soap and water, may also contain it.[1]

Wikipedia credits Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital with noticing in the 1950s that DHA given as part of an oral treatment stained skin brown. The first commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, appeared in 1959, followed by Coppertone's QT in 1960; early products were widely criticised for orange tones. Reformulated products and automated spray-tan booths broadened the market from the late 1990s.[3][4]

Spray tanning delivers a DHA mist over the whole body by hand-held sprayer, booth or technician, and typically lasts about 5 to 10 days.[3] Bronzer powders and lotions are applied with brushes, sponges or hands and are the same product category used in makeup routines. T Nation forum members who compete in bodybuilding shows describe using bronzer or a spray tan before stage appearances and note that the colour is washed off in the shower afterwards.[7]

The FDA approves DHA for external use only. The agency recommends that customers shield eyes, lips and mucous membranes and avoid ingesting or inhaling DHA; spray booths and airbrushing can make that contact hard to avoid, and the 2018 review calls for more safety studies given how widely DHA is used.[1]

Sunless tanners are regulated as cosmetics and, unlike sunscreens, give no protection from UV. Wikipedia says any SPF in a tanner wears off within hours.[1][3] A 2007 study led by Katinka Jung reported that DHA-treated skin produced more free radicals under sun exposure; Wikipedia advises limiting sun for a day after application, and notes a 2004 study that found DNA damage in cultured cells exposed to DHA.[3][4] The EU's scientific committee on consumer safety judged DHA spray tanning not to pose a risk in 2010, an opinion Wikipedia says was criticised for relying on industry-linked studies.[3]

DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis, and fragrances and other bronzer ingredients are common contact allergens; a 2011 survey of 5,416 skin and cosmetic products listed on a US pharmacy chain's website tallied allergen use across categories including blushers and bronzers.[3][5]

Wikipedia separates bronzers from other tanning approaches: oral carotenoids such as beta-carotene and canthaxanthin, which tint skin with high chronic intake and have been linked to harms such as canthaxanthin-associated eye and liver problems; tyrosine 'accelerators', which it says lack supporting data; and melanotan peptides, which health agencies have warned about as unlicensed products since 2007.[3]

No trials have tested caramel bronzers specifically. Research is limited to reviews and laboratory work on the ingredient most often paired with them: a 2018 review of DHA and a 2005 review of spray-on tanning.[1][2] The 2007 free-radical study and the 2004 cell-culture study on DHA are described in Wikipedia's coverage rather than as trials of finished bronzers.[3]

timeline.event: Eva Wittgenstein notices DHA stains skin brown at Cincinnati Children's Hospital.[3]
Reformulated products and automated spray-tan booths expand the sunless-tanning market.[3]
Cell-culture study reports DHA-induced DNA damage.[3]
Jung and colleagues report increased free radical formation in DHA-treated skin under sun exposure.[3]

Journal of Drugs in Dermatology publishes a DHA review.[1]

lore.intro: Bronzers come up in bodybuilding and physique forums mainly as a competition-day colour, and in appearance communities as one option for a golden tone. Claims about them are discussed against the background of sunless-tanning research.[7][6]

claims.claim: Tanning beds or sun exposure are 'pointless' as a base for stage colour; bronzer or spray tan does the work.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster preparing for a first bodybuilding show wrote that a sun or bed base does not get competitors near the colour needed and that bronzer or spray tan is what matters.[6]
claims.experts: Research on bronzers for competition use has not been published; sunless tanners are regulated as cosmetics and give no UV protection, while UV tanning carries well-documented skin-cancer risk.[1][3]

claims.claim: A spray tan or bronzer lets you see a finished tan the same day, washable if it looks wrong.
claims.believers: A T Nation member describes being spray tanned in the morning, avoiding water and sweat, and then showering off the bronzer in the evening to see the final colour.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says bronzers wash off with soap and water while DHA colour fades over about 3 to 10 days as the outer skin layer sheds.[3][4]

claims.claim: Sunless tans are a safe route to a tanned look.
claims.believers: Proponents point to the lack of UV exposure and describe DHA tans as the safer alternative.[2]
claims.experts: A 2005 review calls spray-on tanning a generally safe alternative, while the 2018 DHA review and the FDA note external-use-only approval and call for more safety study; a 2007 study found more free radical formation in DHA-treated skin under sun exposure.[1][2][3]

claims.claim: Tanning pills or carotenoid intake can colour the skin like a bronzer.
claims.believers: Some appearance-forum users discuss beta-carotene or similar nutrients as a way to a warmer skin tone.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says chronic high-dose carotenoids can tint skin but notes harms associated with canthaxanthin tanning pills, and that the FDA has not approved them for tanning.[3]
